newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS-Exceptionals buoy Swire 1996 results.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Exceptionals buoy Swire 1996 results.

text.p: Swire Pacific Ltd posted a strong profit rise of almost 19 percent in 1996, buoyed by exceptionals, and said it was going to focus on topping up its land bank to underpin its property trading operations.
But most analysts said the results were somewhat disappointing when the exceptional profits were stripped out.
Swire chairman Peter Sutch and executive director Keith Kerr both emphasised the company's intention to buy land for residential development.
"It is a top priority. It is absolutely our intention to replenish our land bank and Keith and I have many irons in the fire," Sutch said at a briefing on the company's 1996 profits.
Kerr said the company was "very aware of the need to maintain a sizeable land bank".
In its results, Swire said trading profits from the sale of residential and commercial properties had declined in 1996.

Swire, a conglomerate whose interests span aviation, property, industry, trading, marine services and insurance, posted a 18.6 percent rise in 1996 net profit to HK$7.65 billion (US$988 million), including a HK$1.58 billion exceptional gain.

The gain comprised HK$1.05 billion from the sale of an 80 percent interest in a unit which holds the JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, a HK$468 million gain from the sale of an effective 10.65 percent in the direct interest in Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd and HK$59 million profit from the transfer of business from Hong Kong Aircraft Engineering Co Ltd to a joint venture company formed with Rolls-Royce Plc.
Salomon Brothers analyst Anil Daswani said the results were a little bit lower than he had expected, excluding exceptionals.
"I'm a little bit disappointed," Daswani said.
Morgan Stanley analyst Mike Warren said the net profit result was slightly below his own prediction of HK$7.87 billion.
But the result was "not too far out of step with our expectations," Warren said.
ING Barings analyst Mark Simpson said the result looked all right, and was about four percent above his forecast.
Swire warned that the 1996 exceptional gains were unlikely to be repeated in 1997.
Property contributed HK$4.571 billion to group net profits, or almost 60 percent of the total, and 12.7 percent up on 1995.
Aviation contributed HK$2.279 billion to profits, compared to HK$1.831 billion the previous year.
Operating profit from property investment came to HK$3.407 billion, up 9.6 percent on 1995, while property trading came to HK$1.469 billion, down 1.1 per cent on the previous year.
Turnover fell to HK$38.356 billion, compared with HK$53.656 billion in 1995, and airline services and airline catering operating profits were HK$1.231 billion, down 67.3 percent on 1995.

Sutch said lower turnover was due to the shrinking of Swire's stake in Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd to 43.86 percent from 52.63 percent. The airline issued new shares to China-backed conglomerate CITIC Pacific Ltd last June.
This meant Swire could not consolidate the contribution from Cathay Pacific and associates, he said.
Sutch said concerns over Cathay Pacific might have been one factor in Swire shares underperforming the Hang Seng Index this year.
"Talk of (high) fuel prices, pressure on yields, weakness of the yen, I think, flowed through from the Cathay Pacific share price into the Swire Pacific one," Sutch said.
